say: Today we are treasure hunters inside the times tables. The 6, 7, 8 and 9 tables are full of hidden patterns. If you can spot a pattern, you can use it to check answers and to find answers you have never learnt.
We are going to count round the group up to 40. The 7s strip is on the screen. When it is a number in the 7 times table, do not say it: hold up an open palm. That is a Buzz! Two rounds only.
Which numbers did we Buzz? What do you notice about them?
I write the 6 times table and look only at the last digit: 6, 2, 8. If I join the dots in order, what shape? Will it ever touch an odd digit?
stuck: Stuck: write the table down the side of your page first, then circle the last digit of each answer.
Confused: "Look only at the ones digit. 6 × 3 = 18, so we join to the 8."

Ready for more: the Go further what-if on the slide (the 5s and the 9s). Or try the 7s and the 3s and compare. (The 6s are done together on the shared screen; each pair makes just ONE more circle, the 4s.)

say: "Look at the 8 times table: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48 … The last digits go 8, 6, 4, 2, 0, then 8, 6, 4, 2, 0 again. So the pattern repeats every 5."
"What is the last digit of 8 × 23? 8 × 20 ends in 0, so only 8 × 3 matters. 8 × 3 = 24, so 8 × 23 ends in 4. Check: 8 × 23 = 184. Yes."
"I do not know 6 × 8 by heart? I split the array: 5 rows of 8 is 40, one more row of 8 is 8, so 6 × 8 = 48. For 9 × 7 I can do 10 sevens, which is 70, and take one 7 away: 63."

do: Ask: "What pattern do you notice? Does it work every time? Test one more."
Ask: "Which facts do you already know that could help you?"
Ask: "How do you know you have found every way? What order did you go in?"
stuck: Hint 1: "Write the table in order and look at the ones digits only."
Hint 2: "Split the big fact into two smaller facts you know, then add."
Hint 3: "For a grid puzzle, start with a number that can only be made in one way, like 81 or 49."

say: "Why is every answer in the 6 times table even?"
"Why does the 7 times table have odd and even answers?"
"Which is bigger, 6 × 8 or 7 × 7? Can you see why they are so close?"
ask: "Why is every answer in the 6 times table even?"

6 groups can always be put into 3 pairs of groups, so nothing is left over: the answer is even. With 7 groups one group has no partner, so when each group is odd the answer is odd. Extra question: 7 × 7 = 49 is 1 more than 6 × 8 = 48 (do not explain it fully).

say: "You found patterns, tested them and explained why they work. That is exactly what mathematicians do."

p3l3-title.note: Objective: Find and explain patterns in the 6, 7, 8 and 9 times tables, use last-digit patterns, split an array into facts we know, and solve grid and list puzzles in a careful order. Heuristics taught: look for a pattern; make a systematic list. Materials: Multiplication square (1 to 10), dot paper, coloured pencils, a ruler, mini whiteboards. Online: Tutor draws on the digit-circle slide. Each child draws 10 dots round a circle (like a clock) labelled 0 to 9, and has dot paper and coloured pencils. Time plan (90 minutes, with a named 3-minute float inside talk time): opening 0 to 1.5, sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 5 (own paper, nobody marked, one show-me for both), warm-up game 5 to 8 (two rounds) and three quick questions 8 to 11, explore 11 to 25.5 (a Go further what-if is on the explore slide from the start; pairs go to pre-assigned breakout rooms), teaching 25.5 to 36.5 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 36.5 to 41.5, worksheet 41.5 to 70.5 (page 1 in pairs, short teaching, page 2 on their own, a 60-second self-check slide after each page; after question 3 of page 1 any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation; from minute 67.5 everyone chooses), talk time 70.5 to 78.5 (volunteers first, pass is fine), exit ticket 78.5 to 84.5, look back 84.5 to 87.5, stamp and close 87.5 to 90. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child; the tutor never announces who is on which page and invites the whole group, never one child. If the class is behind, children finish the last question of each page at home; the check slides cover it. SPINE: Today's tool is Spot the pattern. Look for what repeats or changes by the same amount, then say the rule. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p3l3-tool.note: SPINE: Show for about 20 seconds, inside the opening. Today's tool is Spot the pattern. Look for what repeats or changes by the same amount, then say the rule. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p3l3-warmcheck.note: Minutes 1.5 to 5. Sneak-peek puzzles: two small puzzles on ideas we have not learnt yet. Give about 1 minute for each puzzle, then say "say it" ONCE for both: children say both answers together on three (about 30 seconds); nothing is held up to the camera. SAY: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome and so is I do not know. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an ACCESS puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Children write both answers on their own paper and say them together on three (once for both puzzles); nothing is held up to the camera. No private messages. Never answers read out, never "who got it?". Do not show the answers on the slide now. Puzzle 1 answer (tutor only): 49 and 63. Listen for: Look along the table: 49 and 63 are there; 54 is not. Puzzle 2 answer (tutor only): 84 and 36. Listen for: 14 is double 7, so double 42 = 84. 6 × 6 is one 6 less than 6 × 7: 42 − 6 = 36. Come back to puzzle 2 at talk time: "Now we know the idea, how could it help?" (volunteers only). Invite the WHOLE group once, never one child; this is an invitation, not a ranking, and any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation after question 3 of page 1. Never announce who is on which page, and never split pairs unless both children agree.

p3l3-warm1.note: Minutes 5 to 8. Buzz! Play TWO short rounds only: round 1 counts from 1 to 40 starting with the first name on screen, round 2 starts from a different child. Count round the group (online: in the order of the names on screen) from 1 to 40. Any number in the 7 times table is replaced by an open palm (a Buzz) (and the word "Buzz" if you like): the 7s strip stays on the screen, so nobody has to remember the table. Play it light and kind. If someone misses a Buzz or says the number, say "That is a tricky one, let us check on the strip" and carry on from that number; never start again from 1 and never name who missed. Click to show the 7s Buzz numbers at the end and read them together. Only the 7s are played here (the 6s and 8s rounds are not needed today). Ask volunteers: "What do you notice about the Buzz numbers?" (they go up by 7 each time; the last digits are 7, 4, 1, 8, 5). Watch for children who count on their fingers from 0 each time: encourage them to add 7 to the last Buzz.

p3l3-warm2.note: Minutes 8 to 11. Children write on whiteboards and show together, then click to reveal. For each one ask: "How did you work it out? Which fact did you use?" Answers: 1) 42 2) 81 3) 8. Three quick questions only. The question "Which is bigger: 6 × 8 or 7 × 7?" (7 × 7 = 49 is 1 more than 6 × 8 = 48) has moved to talk time.

p3l3-explore1.note: Minutes 11 to 21. Pairs work with: dot paper or plain paper, coloured pencils, a ruler. Each pair draws three digit circles. Do the whole 6s circle WITH the class on the shared screen: 6 × 1 = 6, so start at 6; 6 × 2 = 12, last digit 2, so draw a line from 6 to 2, and so on (about 2 minutes). Then each pair makes ONE more circle, the 4s, in a different colour (about 6 minutes of pair work). The 8s and the comparison with the 4s and 6s are the Go further card or take-home. Online: children draw circles on paper and describe them aloud. Ready for more: the Go further card on the slide (the 8s, then the 5s and the 9s). Or try the 7s and the 3s (they make the same 10-pointed star, which uses every digit). GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of explore, so nobody waits): Do the 8s too. Which tables make the same shape? Then the 5s and 9s: how many dots does each touch? Answer: The 8s make the same 5-sided shape as the 2s (8, 6, 4, 2, 0). The 5s touch only 2 dots (5 and 0). The 9s touch all 10 dots, going round the other way, like the 1s, because each 9 times answer is 1 less in the ones place than the one before. Any pair may choose it as soon as their first task is done; do not say who is ready for it. Online: pairs are in pre-assigned breakout rooms (set up before the lesson, auto-move in and auto-close with a timer, about 45 seconds per move). Visit each breakout room at least once while the pairs work (about 1 minute per room).

p3l3-explore2.note: Minutes 21 to 25.5. Gather the pairs for these three questions. Take ideas before giving any answer and ask "How could we test that?" Answers: 1) The 4s and the 6s make the same 5-pointed star, going round opposite ways (4, 8, 2, 6, 0 and 6, 2, 8, 4, 0). (Pairs who also did the 8s: the 2s and the 8s make the same 5-sided shape.) 2) Every answer in the 6 times table is even: 6 groups can always be put into 3 pairs of groups, so nothing is left over. 3) The 7s, because 3 + 7 = 10, just like 4 + 6 and 2 + 8. Let a pair test it on a new circle. Keep the circles: we use last digits again in the teaching.

p3l3-teach1.note: Teach the first heuristic: LOOK FOR A PATTERN. Say: "Mathematicians notice a pattern, test it, then explain why it works. That is our slogan!" Click 1 shows the last digits. Ask: "What do you notice?" before click 2. Click 3: test the pattern on numbers beyond the table. Click 4: explain why: 8 = 10 − 2, so every time we add 8 the ones digit goes down by 2 (and the tens digit goes up). Think-aloud: "Look at the 8 times table: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48 … The last digits go 8, 6, 4, 2, 0, then again. So the pattern repeats every 5." Do not teach the 9s patterns here: children discover them in worksheet Q1.

p3l3-try1.note: Worked example and your turn in one slide (the old separate worked-example slide was merged here). Think-aloud: "8 × 20 ends in 0, so only 8 × 3 matters. 8 × 3 = 24, so 8 × 23 ends in 4. Check: 8 × 23 = 184. Yes." Stress: "Only the ones digit of 23 matters for the last digit." Ask: "What is the last digit of 8 × 33? 8 × 43?" (still 4). Then whiteboards, say the answer together on three, then click. a) 6 × 4 = 24, so 4 (6 × 14 = 84). b) 8 × 7 = 56, so 6 (8 × 17 = 136). c) 9 × 2 = 18, so 8 (9 × 12 = 108). Ask a child to explain c out loud using the words "only the ones digit".

p3l3-teach2.note: Teach: use facts you know. Show the array on dot paper (or draw it). Cover the bottom row with a ruler: "How many dots above the ruler? 5 rows of 8 is 40. How many below? One row of 8. Altogether 40 + 8 = 48." Click through the steps. Common slip: giving 40 as the answer and forgetting to add the second part. Ask: "Where else could I cut it?" (3 rows and 3 rows: 24 + 24 = 48).

p3l3-we2.note: Click through. Way 2 is the "one too many" trick: 9 of something is 10 of it, take one away. Think-aloud: "For 9 × 7 I can do 10 sevens, which is 70, and take one 7 away: 63. I check it the other way: 35 + 28 is also 63." Two ways that agree is a strong check.

p3l3-try2.note: Whiteboards. Accept any correct split. a) 5 × 7 + 1 × 7 = 35 + 7 = 42. b) 5 × 6 + 3 × 6 = 30 + 18 = 48. c) 10 × 8 − 8 = 72, or 5 × 8 + 4 × 8 = 40 + 32 = 72. Ask two children with different splits to show theirs.

p3l3-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Checking the 9s table only by "the digits add up to 9" (81 passes, but 9 × 8 is 72). (2) Splitting an array and then giving one part as the answer (40 instead of 40 + 16). (3) Missing or repeating ways in a list because the rows are not tried in order 2, 3, 4, 5 …

p3l3-break.note: Five minutes. Call 6 × 3, 7 × 2, 8 × 3, 9 × 2. Online: children stay in view of the camera and jump on the spot.

p3l3-ws1.note: Minutes 41.5 to 54. Pairs work together. Walk around and ask "What pattern do you notice? Does it work every time?" For Q1b push for the pattern that catches Ali: the tens digit is one less than the number of nines. For Q2a pairs test only the 3, 6 and 9 tables (6 gives only even digits) and may need the digit circles from the explore. PAGE 1 CLOCK (41.5 to 54): about 2 minutes to hand out and get started, then pairs auto-move to their pre-assigned breakout rooms (about 45 seconds), about 9 minutes of pair work with the room timer on, and auto-close back to the main room (about 45 seconds). Visit each room once. Items not finished are finished at home; the check slide covers them.

p3l3-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1a also accept: the tens digit is 1 less than the number of nines. Q1b: the digit-sum test alone is not enough, because 81 also has digits adding to 9; the tens-digit pattern shows 9 × 8 must be in the 70s. Q2a: the 3s go 3, 6, 9, 2, 5, 8, 1, 4, 7, 0 and the 9s go 9, 8, 7 … 0. The 6s give only even digits (6, 2, 8, 4, 0). Ask why the even tables cannot work (all their answers are even) and why the 5s cannot (only 5 and 0). Q2b: 7 × 6 = 42 ends in 2; 7 × 46 = 322. Q3b: any correct split, e.g. 5 × 6 + 4 × 6 or 10 × 6 − 6. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and tick the corrected page against the answer slide (nothing is held up to the camera). Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l3-teachlist.note: Teach the second heuristic: MAKE A SYSTEMATIC LIST. Before worksheet Q5 (36 chairs). Click to add each row while children say whether it works: "Can 18 be shared into 4 equal rows?" (No: 4 rows of 4 is 16, 2 are left over.) Point out the pairs: 2 rows of 9 and 9 rows of 2, 3 rows of 6 and 6 rows of 3. Ask: "How do we know we have them all?" (We tried every number of rows in order.) Do not do 36: that is Q5.

p3l3-teachgrid.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4 is a 3 by 3 grid puzzle). Ask first: "Which number can be made in only ONE way with numbers from 1 to 10?" Children list factor pairs: 72 = 8 × 9 only; 63 = 7 × 9 only; 42 = 6 × 7 only. Click order: steps 1 to 3, then the finished grid fades in, then step 4. On the worksheet the hint gives the starting facts (81 = 9 × 9 and 56 = 7 × 8), and Q4 is marked (if time): show this slide quickly, and only children who start Q4 need it. Children who skip Q4 can use the time to start Q5.

p3l3-teachboth.note: Teach before worksheet Q6. Strategy: list the numbers for ONE clue in order, then test the other clues one at a time. Ask: "Why list the 7s, not the 3s?" (There are fewer of them, so the list is shorter.) Children may notice 21, 42, 63, 84 go up in 21s. Do not do Q6 (6 and 8) here.

p3l3-ws2.note: Children work alone. Q4 is an (if time) item but comes first on the page: say that any child may start with Q5 (the compulsory question) and come back to Q4. Page 2 is a little longer in this lesson so that Q5 can be done without hurry. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson. For Q4, if a child is stuck after a few minutes, ask "Which number is in only one times table up to 10 × 10?" (81).

p3l3-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains. Q4: start with 81 = 9 × 9, so the middle row and the last column are 9. Then 56 = 7 × 8 and 48 = 6 × 8 share the first column, so it is 8 (7 × 7 = 49 rules out 7), giving rows 7 and 6; 36 = 6 × 6 gives the middle column 6. Q5: 5, 7, 8, 10 and 11 rows do not work. The number of ways is odd because 6 × 6 pairs with itself. Q6: list 16, 24, 32 … 96 and test each for ÷ 6: 24, 48, 72, 96. Digit sums 6, 12, 9, 15, so 48. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and tick the corrected page against the answer slide (nothing is held up to the camera). Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l3-stretch.note: For children who choose Think harder. Answers: 1) (a) 49 is 1 more than 48. (b) 64 is 1 more than 63. (c) 56 is 2 more than 54. The closer the two numbers are to each other, the bigger the answer. 2) 1: the last digits go 9, 1, 9, 1 (9 × 9 × 9 × 9 = 6561). 3) 4 or 9: 6 × 4 = 24 and 6 × 9 = 54; check every digit 0 to 9, no other one gives a last digit of 4.

p3l3-challenge.note: Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. Answers: 1) Rows 6 and 7, columns 7 and 8. Start with 49: it can only be 7 × 7. 2) 4 answers: 18, 48, 78, 108. The last digits 6, 2, 8, 4, 0 repeat every 5, so 8 comes once in every 5 answers.

p3l3-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried the Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you notice? What do we know? Which number should we start with? Could we use a pattern instead of writing all 20 answers? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p3l3-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: the same idea as the worksheet grid: find the number with only one factor pair. Q2: children who wrote all 20 answers are right too; ask them to look for the shortcut. 6 × 13 = 78 and 6 × 18 = 108.

p3l3-talk.note: Minutes 70.5 to 78.5. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Praise the reasons, not only the answers. Extra question (moved here from the quick questions): "Which is bigger, 6 × 8 or 7 × 7? Can you see why they are so close?" (49 is 1 more than 48; do not explain it fully.) Expected: 6 groups can always be put into 3 pairs of groups, so nothing is left over and the answer is even. With 7 groups one group has no partner, so when each group is odd (7 × 3 = 21) the answer is odd. Use counters in 6 or 7 groups to show it. TALK TIME FLOAT: this part holds the lesson's named 3-minute float. If you are behind, shorten talk time (one discussion question, then the partner share); if you are on time, use the full time for the second question and the return to sneak-peek puzzle 2. Never take time from the exit ticket, look back or stamp. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a pass is always fine and so is sharing with a partner. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and nobody is told they were wrong in front of the group. Nobody is called on by name.

p3l3-exit.note: Minutes 78.5 to 84.5. Answer: 2. Only 6 × 7 = 42 decides the last digit, because 6 × 40 ends in 0. (6 × 47 = 282.) Extension: draw last-digit circles for all the tables from 1 to 9 and group the tables that make the same shape. Answers stay on the child’s own paper and are ticked against the answer slide. Never mark or read out answers in front of the group. Reflection (look back) follows on the next slide: allow 3 minutes, 2 for the children plus a short share.

p3l3-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 84.5 to 87.5. Start the timer (90 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 87.5 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new.
